The Processes tab allows you to submit tasks one at a time. This manual approach is ideal when you are exploring different Apps, inspecting intermediate results, or testing configurations on a single subject. However, once you have identified your optimal processing steps and need to scale across tens, hundreds, or thousands of subjects, submitting them individually is neither practical nor reproducible. Brainlife solves this through Pipelines and Automations (rule-based stream processing). Instead of requiring you to write and maintain complex workflow scripts (like Snakemake, Nextflow, or Nipype DAGs) that run once and fail if any single participant errors out, Brainlife evaluates independent Automations continuously across your project. ---

Think of a Brainlife pipeline as an intelligent assembly line: 1. Independent Rules: Each automation defines an App to run, its configuration parameters, required input criteria (datatypes, tags, subject filters), and expected output tags. 2. Continuous Event-Driven Evaluation: Brainlife continuously monitors your project. Whenever a subject or session possesses all required input datasets and has not yet produced the designated output, a new process is automatically dispatched. 3. Automatic Derivative Archiving: As soon as an App finishes running, its output datasets are archived into your project and immediately satisfy the input requirements for downstream automations. 4. Fault Tolerance & Resilience: If a particular subject fails (e.g., due to scan artifacts or motion), only that specific subject stops at that step. The rest of your cohort continues through the pipeline uninterrupted. You can inspect logs, resolve the issue, and once the missing output is produced, downstream automations pick it right back up. ---

To view and manage your project pipelines: 1. Open your project on Brainlife. 2. Select the 3. Processing tab from the top navigation bar. 3. In the sub-navigation toggle, switch from Summary or Processes to Pipeline. If your project does not contain any datasets yet, you will be prompted to first add or copy data into the project under the 2. Data tab before configuring automations. ---

To add a new rule to your pipeline, click the + Automation button in the top-right toolbar. This opens the Add New Automation to Pipeline wizard. The creation flow guides you through four sequential steps:

Browse or search the Brainlife App catalog to select the App you want to automate (e.g., FreeSurfer, FSL BET, Tractoflow, etc.). You can search by App name, keywords, or modalities, and toggle compatibility filters to view only Apps that match your project's staged datatypes.

Configure the parameters and arguments for the chosen App: - Adjust default numeric values, flags, and configuration toggles required for your analysis. - Expand the Advanced section if your analysis requires specialized execution flags or custom script options.

This step defines the matching criteria Brainlife will use to select datasets for each subject and session: - Required Datatypes: Review the expected input datatypes (e.g. neuro/anat/t1w, neuro/dwi). - Datatype Tags & Annotation Filters: If your project contains multiple datasets of the same datatype for a subject (e.g., multiple T1w runs or sessions), add specific datatype tags or annotation tags to resolve ambiguity and specify exactly which dataset to use. - Parent Project Overrides: If the input datasets reside in another project (such as a shared raw data repository), you can specify a project override to read data directly from the parent project without copying or duplicating files. - Global Subject / Session Filters: Expand the Global Subject/Session Filters panel to restrict the automation to specific subjects or sessions using regular expressions: - Subject Filter: Enter a regex pattern (e.g., ^100 to process only subjects whose IDs begin with 100, or sub-(01|02|03) for specific cohorts). - Session Filter: Enter a regex pattern to limit processing to specific sessions (e.g., 01 or ses-baseline). - Live Match Counter: A real-time badge indicates how many subjects/datasets in your project currently match your filter criteria.

Specify how generated derivatives should be identified: - Output Dataset Tags (Annotations): Add descriptive tags to the generated outputs (e.g., acpc_aligned, freesurfer7). - Output Descriptions: Optionally provide a label or description for downstream tracking. Tagging your outputs is strongly recommended. Output tags distinguish datasets generated by this specific automation from other Apps producing the same datatype, and they prevent accidental duplicate runs while enabling downstream automations to target this exact derivative. Click Create to activate the automation and add it to your pipeline. ---

As your analysis grows in complexity, you can group related automations together: 1. Click the + Automation Group button in the pipeline toolbar. 2. Enter a descriptive name (e.g., Structural Preprocessing, Diffusion Processing, or Network Analysis). 3. Once created, groups appear on the canvas and in the sidebar list. 4. You can collapse or expand groups to keep your workflow clean and focused. 5. Move individual automations into or out of groups via the automation action menu (Move to group). ---

The pipeline page provides an interactive, visual flowchart canvas powered by an automated graph layout engine: - Nodes: Each card represents an automation App, showing its icon, name, active status, and live subject processing counters. - Connections (Edges): Directed lines automatically connect Apps when an output datatype and tag match downstream input requirements, showing you the end-to-end data flow at a glance. - Canvas Controls: Pan by dragging, zoom with your mouse wheel or the mini-map controls, and click nodes to open detailed inspectors. - Collapsible Automations Sidebar: Click the sidebar toggle on the left to reveal a searchable, ordered list of all automations and groups in your project. - View Settings: Click the View Settings button to toggle options such as Show Inactive Automations or customize canvas display preferences. ---

Clicking on any automation card in the flowchart opens the Automation Details modal, which breaks down all subjects into four clear categories: | Status Group | Description | | :--- | :--- | | Waiting | Subjects that have not run yet because required input datasets or upstream prerequisites are not yet available. | | Processing | Tasks that have met all prerequisites and are currently requested, queued, or running on compute resources. | | Complete | Subjects that have finished processing successfully and whose output datasets are safely archived. | | Attention | Subjects requiring user attention, including failed tasks or cases with ambiguous matching inputs (e.g., multiple matching datasets where tags are needed to distinguish them). | From the Automation Details modal, you can: - Toggle Active / Inactive: Use the switch to temporarily pause or resume automatic job submission. - View in Processes: Click the list icon to jump directly to the Processes tab with filters pre-set to show all tasks associated with this automation. - Edit Automation: Click the pencil icon to modify configuration settings, input filters, or output tags. - Delete Automation: Remove the rule from your pipeline. ---

If you need to change configurations or update parameters on an existing automation: 1. Open the automation details and toggle the status switch to Inactive so no new jobs are submitted with the old parameters. 2. Click the Edit (pencil) button to adjust your App settings or filters. 3. If the change alters data outputs (e.g., different resolution or registration target), navigate to the Processes tab or Data tab to clean up any obsolete tasks or outputs generated with the old configuration. 4. Toggle the automation back to Active to resume processing. Brainlife will automatically submit a task whenever a subject has valid inputs but no matching archived output. If you remove an existing task or output dataset while an automation remains Active, Brainlife will automatically re-queue and re-run that subject. If you do not want it re-submitted, deactivate the automation first.

While Pipelines are designed for automated batch processing across large cohorts, the Processes interface allows for hands-on, on-demand execution. A Process is a workspace instance where you stage specific input datasets, execute Apps one at a time, inspect intermediate results, and link tools together into custom analysis workflows. ---

To manage on-demand tasks in your project: 1. Open your project on Brainlife. 2. Select the 3. Processing tab from the top navigation bar. 3. In the sub-navigation toggle bar, switch between Summary, Pipeline, and Processes. The Summary view provides an operational overview of all compute activity across your project: - Action Status Counters: Real-time status cards tracking tasks that Need action, Running jobs, Failed runs, Completed tasks, and Active automations. - Resources in Use: Direct visibility into cluster queue allocations and resource utilization across connected HPC environments. ---
A typical process workflow consists of creating a process, staging data, running an App through the 4-step wizard, and tracking execution:

section: Step 1: Creating a Process & Staging Input Data
content: Processing begins by staging the datasets you want to analyze: 1. From the Processes sub-tab, click + New Process to open the creation dialog. 2. Enter a descriptive Name (e.g., Preprocess Anatomical) and optional description. 3. In the Add Data to Process modal, check the boxes next to the participant datasets you wish to import from your project's repository. 4. Click Import Data Objects (e.g., IMPORT 1 DATA OBJECTS). Brainlife stages the selected data into your process workspace. 5. Click on the staged dataset node or task entry to inspect its metadata, staging logs, and event history in the task inspector dialog:

Once input data is staged, click + Add App on the process canvas or action toolbar to launch the execution wizard: 1. Select App Search or filter the Brainlife App catalog. You can toggle "Only show apps compatible with staged data" to immediately identify algorithms that accept your staged datatypes (e.g., FSL Anat (T1), FreeSurfer, fMRIPrep). 2. Configure App Settings Adjust default algorithmic parameters, threshold values, and processing flags required for your experiment. 3. Select Inputs Map your staged input datasets to the specific input slots required by the App. The wizard verifies datatype compatibility and tags automatically. 4. Configure Outputs Specify user-defined output tags and annotations (e.g., acpc_aligned, preprocessed) so the resulting derivatives are clearly labeled when archived into your project repository. Click Submit to dispatch the task to the compute orchestrator. ---

Brainlife's orchestrator, Amaretti, dispatches your task to an optimal computing resource (HPC cluster, cloud VM, or campus grid) and monitors its lifecycle: | Status | Meaning | | :--- | :--- | | Requested | The job is queued in Brainlife's system and waiting for an available computing resource that matches the task's hardware requirements. | | Running | A compute resource has been assigned, input data has been transferred, and the job is actively executing in a containerized environment (Singularity/Docker). | | Finished | The job completed with return code 0. All output datasets are automatically validated, cataloged, and archived into your project's 2. Data tab. | | Failed | The job exited with an error. You can inspect the execution logs (stdout, stderr) in the side panel to troubleshoot the issue. | | Removed | To conserve cluster storage, the temporary scratch work directory on the remote cluster is automatically purged after 25 days. Your archived output datasets remain safe and permanently stored. | ---

The Processes view provides a high-density, faceted table designed for tracking multiple tasks: - Faceted Filters: Quickly filter jobs by status (Requested, Running, Finished, Failed), App name, submitter, execution resource, or date. - Batch Selection: Select multiple tasks to restart or delete failed jobs. - Side-Panel Inspector: Clicking on any process row opens a sliding drawer on the right side of the screen containing: - Live Log Stream: View real-time terminal output, standard output (stdout), and error output (stderr). - Task Files & Raw Output: Browse and download all intermediate log files, configuration files, and script outputs. - Compute Resource Information: Details about the host cluster, walltime duration, memory consumption, and exit code. ---

For complex, multi-step workflows that involve chaining multiple Apps together, Brainlife Connects provides the Interactive Process Editor: 1. In the Processes table, click the Process Editor link or navigate to /projects/:projectId/processing/processes/:instanceId/editor. 2. The editor launches a visual, interactive ReactFlow canvas representing the workflow Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) for that specific process instance: - Data Nodes: Represent staged raw input datasets or intermediate derivatives generated by Apps. - App Nodes: Represent individual tool executions (e.g., App 1: Skull Stripping $\rightarrow$ App 2: Registration $\rightarrow$ App 3: Tractography). - Dependency Edges: Visually map the flow of data objects from App outputs to downstream App inputs. 3. You can click on any node in the graph to inspect intermediate outputs, check task status, configure parameters, or attach new Apps directly into the pipeline graph.

Projects are the primary collaborative workspaces on Brainlife. Within a project, you organize datasets, configure automated pipelines, execute computational tasks, launch interactive cloud Jupyter notebooks, and publish citable data releases. You can browse your own workspaces by selecting My Projects (/projects?scope=mine) or explore community research workspaces under Public Projects (/projects?scope=public). ---

To create a new project: 1. Click My Projects in the left sidebar navigation. 2. Click the New Project button in the upper-right corner. 3. Fill in the project details: - Title: A clear name for your project (e.g., Developmental Connectome Study). - Description: A summary of your research goals, participant cohorts, or analytical techniques. 4. Click Create project. Upon creation, you will be navigated directly to your project workspace. ---
Every standard Brainlife project is organized into five dedicated tabs:

The project homepage provides high-level documentation, metrics, and governance: - Project Metrics & Stats: Immediate summary counters displaying total storage consumption (e.g., 22.8 GB), number of Datasets (7), Participants (7), Processes (2), and active Automation Rules (5). - ReadMe Documentation: Rich Markdown detailing your study protocol, hypotheses, experimental design, and data collection notes. - Automatic App Citations: A consolidated list of bibliographic citations for all computational Apps executed within the project, making it effortless to cite software in scientific publications. - People & Roles: A visual roster of project administrators and contributing members, complete with user avatars, institutional affiliations, and the Add Member management interface. - Computing Resources: A transparent panel listing all registered High-Performance Computing (HPC) clusters (e.g., Karst, Big Red 200, Carbonate, Quartz) authorized to process tasks for this project.

The central data repository for your project (replacing the legacy "Archive"): - Interactive Data Table: View all data objects organized by Subject ID, Session, Datatype, and Tags. - Datatype & Annotation Filters: Filter and search participants or modalities in real time. - Batch Actions: Select multiple datasets to download, delete, edit tags, or stage directly into processing workflows. - Dataset Inspector & Visualizer: Click any dataset row to inspect file hierarchies, review provenance history, or launch in-browser NiiVue WebGL 3D volume and surface visualizers. - Adding Data: Use the Add Project Data button to upload local files, import BIDS datasets via ezBIDS, or copy open-science datasets directly from OpenNeuro, DANDI, BossDB, or EMBER without consuming local bandwidth.

The computational execution engine, divided into three specialized sub-views: - Summary: Live dashboard of project processing health, task completion metrics, and tools to resolve ambiguous inputs. - Pipeline: Visual flowchart canvas to design and monitor rule-based Automations and Automation Groups for continuous batch processing. - Processes: Interactive table of individual compute jobs, sliding raw output log drawers, and the visual Process DAG Editor.

Interactive data science in the cloud: - Launch cloud-hosted Jupyter Notebook instances directly attached to your project data. - Run group statistical models, plot tract profiles, analyze connectome matrices, and generate publication-ready figures without downloading datasets to your local machine.

Data preservation and scientific dissemination: - Snapshot project datasets and group analyses into permanent, citable Releases (Release 1, Release 2). - Automatically assign a DataCite DOI with long-term IU Scholarly Data Archive tape backing and FAIR schema.org metadata. For lightweight repositories primarily focused on raw data hosting or pipeline execution without interactive notebook modeling, Brainlife supports Lean Projects, which streamline the layout into four tabs (1. Overview, 2. Data, 3. Processing, and 4. Publications). ---
Project administrators can manage project configuration at any time by clicking Settings (/projects/:projectId/settings). The settings dashboard is organized into five functional sections:

- Title & Description: Edit the public project name and abstract. - ReadMe: Update the project's Markdown documentation. - Avatar: Upload a custom icon or logo representing your project. - Project Tags: Add keywords (e.g., fMRI, ADHD, Connectomics) for search indexing across Brainlife.

Brainlife provides fine-grained role-based permissions: | Role | Permissions | | :--- | :--- | | Admin | Full control. Can modify project settings, invite/remove members, adjust access policies, assign compute resources, and delete the project. | | Member | Read and write access. Can upload data, stage datasets, submit compute processes, edit automations, and launch analysis notebooks. Cannot alter project membership or delete the project. | | Guest | Read-only access. Can view project overview, browse datasets, and inspect pipeline execution status without making modifications. | Visibility Policies - Public: Any registered Brainlife user can view project details, download archived datasets, and use data as inputs in processing workflows. - Private: Restricted exclusively to project Admins, Members, and Guests. The project is hidden from public listings. - List project summary for all users: Keeps the underlying datasets private to project members while allowing the project title, abstract, and tags to appear in public searches so external researchers can request collaboration.

Protect sensitive or human-subjects data with mandatory electronic agreements: - Add custom Data Access Agreements (DUAs), institutional ethics declarations, or consent forms. - Any researcher (including external users on public projects) must electronically accept your terms before they can download or stage project data.

Manage participant demographic and phenotypic metadata (participants.tsv): - Configure clinical columns such as age, sex, group, diagnosis, or behavioral test scores. - Publish Participant Info: Toggle whether participant metadata is included when publishing data releases. - Strict privacy safeguards warn against including any Protected Health Information (PHI) or personal identifiers.

Designate computing clusters and execution queues: - Select which HPC or cloud compute resources (such as Indiana University HPC clusters, Slate, Jetstream, or private Slurm clusters) are authorized to execute jobs for this project. - Restrict job submissions to specific lab allocations or project billing accounts. ---

section: Storage Architecture: Standard vs. Direct S3
content: Brainlife projects support two underlying storage models: 1. Standard Storage: Datasets are stored in Brainlife's secure distributed cloud storage backed by DataLad and IU tape archives. 2. Direct S3 Storage: For petascale datasets hosted on AWS S3 or compatible object stores, Brainlife projects can link directly to external S3 buckets, allowing pipeline apps to stream and process cloud data in place.

Once you finish processing your datasets and producing your data derivatives, you can publish them directly from Brainlife. Publishing creates a permanent, citable public record of your datasets and group analyses, assigned with a unique Digital Object Identifier (DOI). Publication records are preserved for at least ten years and backed by long-term storage, including the Indiana University Scholarly Data Archive tape archive. Brainlife automatically generates schema.org metadata to maximize discovery, search indexing, and adherence to FAIR data principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable). ---

Every publication created on Brainlife includes: - Permanent URL & Unique DOI: Issued via DataCite, redirecting permanently to your publication page (https://brainlife.io/pubs/ ). - Versioned Releases: A publication can contain multiple sequential releases (e.g., Release 1, Release 2), allowing you to publish new datasets, additional subjects, or updated derivative pipelines over time without losing historical provenance. - One-Click Citation: A pre-formatted citation box with instant BibTeX and text export to make citing your dataset seamless for other researchers. - Interactive Data Explorer & Visualizers: Visitors can browse the dataset hierarchy, inspect file trees, and view 2D/3D visualizations directly in the browser before downloading. - Open Access with Agreement Protection: Public datasets can be browsed and downloaded by anyone without requiring a login, unless your project specifies a Data Access Agreement (in which case users must register and agree to your terms prior to downloading). To maintain scientific reproducibility and uphold DOI registration guarantees with DataCite, publications and releases cannot be deleted directly from the user interface. If you need to retract or remove a publication due to an error, you must contact Brainlife support at brlife@iu.edu. Always review your included datasets and metadata carefully before publishing. ---

To create a new publication from your project: 1. Open your project on Brainlife. 2. Select the Publications tab from the project navigation bar. 3. Click the New Publication button at the top of the page.

Fill in the core metadata for your publication: | Field | Description | Required | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Name | A clear, informative title for the publication or dataset. | Yes | | Description | An abstract summarizing the study, participant demographics, imaging modalities, and intended use cases. | Yes | | License | The data access and re-use license (defaults to CC-BY 4.0). | Yes | | Authors | Ordered list of primary authors with institutional affiliations. Select registered Brainlife users or add names. | Yes (at least one) | | Contributors | Additional team members, curators, or contributors who assisted with the data collection or processing. | No | | Funding Sources | Grant awards and funding agencies (provide Funder name and Award/Grant ID). | No | | Tags | Keywords indicating imaging modalities, disorders, or study techniques (e.g., fMRI, Diffusion, Connectome). | No | | Ontology Topics | Standardized scientific topics from biomedical ontologies to optimize discoverability. | No | | ReadMe | Detailed study documentation written in Markdown (e.g., scan parameters, cohort exclusion criteria, code references). | No |

When you submit the form, a confirmation modal will outline the creation details: - A new DOI is requested and registered with DataCite. - Your publication record is created, and you are automatically redirected to the publication editor where you can associate specific datasets into Releases. ---
Once created, project administrators and members can edit the publication by clicking Edit Publication. The editor is organized into four main sections:
Update any of your initial metadata fields at any time, including title, abstract, authors, contributors, grant numbers, license, tags, and the ReadMe documentation.

Customize the public presentation of your publication: - Custom URL Slug: Define a clean, memorable URL slug (e.g., https://brainlife.io/pubs/my-study-2026). - Banner Image: Upload or select a custom hero banner image for the publication header.

For large-scale, multi-institutional, or multi-modal publications, you can organize your study into Groups. Each group can have dedicated sub-panels for: - Overview: Group-specific descriptions and focus areas. - People: Sub-teams or working groups responsible for specific components. - Data: Modality-specific datasets associated with the group. - Media: Showcase figures, screenshots, and visual assets.

The Releases tab is where you link actual project data to your publication: 1. Click Add new release to create a version (e.g., Release 1). 2. Provide a Release Name and Description detailing what data is included in this snapshot. 3. Under Data Objects, click Add Data Object to select which archived datasets and datatypes from your project should be included in this release. 4. Under Group Analyses, attach any multi-subject group analysis archives (gaarchives) produced in your project. 5. As your study progresses, you can add subsequent releases (Release 2, Release 3) to share newly acquired sessions or updated derivative pipelines. ---

Visitors accessing your publication via its direct URL or DOI will see a comprehensive, modern study portal: - Header & DOI: Displays study title, authors, custom banner, and a persistent badge linking directly to the DataCite DOI. - Citations Card: Formats the publication citation automatically and provides quick buttons to copy the plain text citation or BibTeX snippet. - ReadMe Card: Renders your full Markdown documentation, protocols, and references. - Releases Explorer: - Displays each release in an expandable accordion. - Lists included datatypes, subjects, and sessions. - Features an interactive File Tree Browser allowing visitors to inspect file hierarchies within archived data objects. - Includes integrated Visualizations, enabling users to open 2D/3D interactive visualizers directly from the browser before downloading. - Download Data: Visitors can download individual files or entire datasets. If the project requires data access agreements, visitors will be prompted to log in and sign the required agreement before files can be retrieved. ---

All published datasets on Brainlife are indexed on the global Research / Publications directory (https://brainlife.io/pubs). Researchers worldwide can discover your work by searching: - Study names and author names - Specific imaging modalities and datatypes (e.g., T1w, DWI, MEG, fMRI) - Keywords, diseases, and ontology topics - Associated project licenses

Welcome to Brainlife Connects (connects.brainlife.io )! Brainlife is an open, cloud-based platform for reproducible neuroimaging data analysis, processing pipelines, and scientific publication. This "Getting Started" guide will walk you through the core workflow on Brainlife Connects: 1. Signing up and logging in 2. Key terms to know 3. Navigating the platform 4. Creating a new project 5. Adding data to your project 6. Visualizing data-objects 7. Running processing apps and pipelines 8. Interactive group analysis with notebooks ---

To begin using Brainlife, you need a registered account: 1. Go to the Brainlife authentication page . 2. Choose your preferred login method: Third-Party Providers: Google, GitHub, ORCID, Apple, or your academic institution. Email & Password: Sign up directly with your email address. 3. You can connect multiple login providers to your profile in Settings > Account > Account Settings > Connected Accounts. If you register using a third-party authenticator (such as Google or GitHub), make sure to sign in with that same account every time so you don't inadvertently create multiple profiles. ---
Before diving into project workflows, let's review two fundamental concepts:

A data-object is a specific set of files representing one subject, session, and neuroimaging modality. It is the core unit of data on Brainlife: For example, a neuro/dwi data-object consists of dwi.nii.gz (the 4D diffusion image), dwi.bvecs, and dwi.bvals. A FreeSurfer parcellation output for a subject is a single data-object containing all generated surface and segmentation directories. * Data-objects have immutable data (the underlying raw image files cannot be modified) and mutable metadata (tags, subject IDs, and descriptions can be updated).

Brainlife Apps exchange information through standardized datatypes. Each datatype defines the expected files, directory structure, and metadata for a modality. Colored badges on an App card indicate which datatype an App requires as input and which datatype it generates as output. Datatype tags (such as acpc_aligned, masked, or preprocessed) provide extra specificity so downstream Apps receive the exact input format they need. Browse registered specifications anytime on the Datatypes page . ---

Brainlife Connects provides a streamlined sidebar navigation divided into two primary zones: Me (Personal Workspace): Dashboard: Your unified hub displaying recent task activity, project shortcuts, and processing notifications. My Projects: Projects you administer, contribute to, or follow. My Resources: Compute clusters, HPC resources, or cloud nodes registered for your use. My Datatypes: Custom datatypes you maintain or develop. Explore (Community & Open Science): SKAI: Brainlife's AI-powered neuroimaging assistant to help design workflows, query analyses, and troubleshoot tasks. Public Datasets: Centralized explorer for open neuroscience data, including the Dataset Library, DANDI, EMBER, and BossDB (with direct S3 browsing). Apps: The catalog of public neuroimaging analysis tools, containerized and ready to run. Datatypes: Community-registered datatype standards. Public Projects: Shared open research projects from labs worldwide. Research: Published datasets and reproducibility packages with DOIs. ---

Projects are workspaces where you organize datasets, run compute workflows, launch interactive analyses, and collaborate with your team. 1. In the sidebar menu, click My Projects (/projects?scope=mine). 2. Click the New Project button in the upper right. 3. Fill in the project creation modal: Title: A concise, descriptive name (e.g. Longitudinal Tractography Study). Description: A summary of research questions, cohorts, or methods. 4. Click Create project. Congratulations! Brainlife will create your project and navigate directly to its workspace.

Inside your project, you will find five dedicated tabs: 1. 1. Overview: ReadMe documentation, access control (Admins, Members, Guests), related journal articles, and automatic citations for the Apps used. 2. 2. Data: Interactive table of all project data-objects, metadata filtering, dataset visualizers, and staging actions. 3. 3. Processing: Execution center with three views: Summary (job health and execution stats), Pipeline (automation rules), and Processes (running and completed compute jobs). 4. 4. Analysis: Built-in Jupyter Notebook instances running in the cloud directly against your project data. 5. 5. Publications: Tools to snapshot and permanently publish datasets and pipelines with citable DOIs. ---

Once your project is created, navigate to the 2. Data tab. To add data, click the Add Project Data button at the top right of the data table. You can choose from multiple sources: Copy Data from Public Datasets: Browse thousands of open-access subjects from BossDB, DANDI, OpenNeuro, and the Brainlife Dataset Library, and import them directly into your project with a single click—no local downloading required. Copy Data From another Project: Select any public project or another project you belong to and copy datasets directly into your current workspace. * Upload Data from ezBIDS / Local Files: If you have raw DICOM or NIfTI data on your local machine, convert and organize it using ezBIDS or upload it through the web uploader or Brainlife CLI.

Brainlife Connects makes open neuroscience datasets immediately available without requiring local downloads or manual staging: 1. Explore the Public Datasets Catalog: Navigate to Explore > Public Datasets (/public-datasets). Use the source pills to filter collections by repository (Dataset Library, DANDI, EMBER, BossDB, or OpenNeuro), or search by title and modality. 2. Inspect Collection Data: Click on any collection (such as ADHD200 - KKI) and switch to its 2. DATA tab to inspect all subjects, sessions, and available modalities. 3. Filter Datatypes: Use the Datatype dropdown in the top-right toolbar to isolate specific modalities (such as anat/t1w or func/task). 4. Copy to Project: Click the COPY TO PROJECT button in the upper-right corner. In the dialog: Select which datatypes you need to import. Choose either an Existing project or create a New project. * Click SUBMIT. Brainlife creates virtual DataLad links in your project instantly. ---

You can inspect brain images, segmentations, and tractography results directly in your web browser without downloading multi-gigabyte files to your computer: 1. On the 2. Data tab, your staged data-objects are organized by subject and session, displaying their datatypes, tags, file sizes, and creation dates. 2. Click the Visualize icon (:fa-eye: eyeball) on the right side of any dataset row, or select multiple rows to compare them. 3. Select an available viewer suited for that datatype: Volume Viewer: Slices through 3D/4D anatomical and functional volumes, with support for side-by-side multi-dataset comparison, voxel/world coordinate inspection, and color map thresholds. Freeview / FSLeyes: GPU-accelerated cloud viewers streamed directly to your browser via WebRTC/VNC. * TractView: Interactive 3D white matter tractography and streamline visualizer. 4. The viewer launches in a clean modal overlay, letting you adjust contrasts, toggle overlays, and perform quick visual quality control before launching compute pipelines. ---
To run computational analysis on your data, Brainlife Connects offers two integrated methods: Processes for on-demand task runs and Pipelines for automated batch execution.

1. Go to the 2. Data tab and select the dataset(s) you wish to process using the checkboxes on the left. 2. In the action bar that appears above the table, click Stage to process (or click the List icon on an individual row). 3. Select an existing process or choose to create a new process instance. 4. Open the 3. Processing tab and switch to the Processes sub-view. 5. Click Submit App to search the App catalog for an appropriate analysis tool (for example, FSL Anat (T1) or FreeSurfer for anatomical processing). 6. Configure the App parameters and click Submit. Brainlife's orchestrator (Amaretti ) automatically transfers your data to an optimal computing resource, submits the batch job, and monitors its execution: Requested: The job is queued and waiting for compute resources. Running: The job is actively executing on the designated HPC/cloud cluster. Finished: Execution succeeded! Derivative datasets are automatically added to your project's data catalog. Failed: If an error occurred, expand the task's Raw Output to inspect stdout, stderr, and log files.

If you need to analyze dozens or hundreds of subjects across your project: 1. In the 3. Processing tab, select the Pipeline sub-view. 2. Click the + Automation button to launch the 4-step wizard: - Select App: Choose an App from the catalog. - Configure App Settings: Set fixed runtime flags and arguments. - Configure Inputs: Set datatype tag filters, project overrides, and regex Subject/Session Filters. - Configure Outputs: Add output tags to identify derivatives cleanly. 3. Organize related rules into collapsible groups with + Automation Group. 4. Once active, the automation continuously evaluates your project: whenever subjects matching your criteria are added or upstream derivatives are produced, Brainlife automatically launches the App and archives the outputs. ---

Brainlife Connects integrates statistical analysis directly into your project via the 4. Analysis tab: 1. Click the 4. Analysis tab. 2. Click New analysis to launch an interactive cloud Jupyter Notebook. 3. Choose to start from a blank template or import a published analysis notebook. 4. The notebook runs directly inside your project environment, allowing you to load dataset derivatives, compute group averages, plot tract profiles, and generate figures without downloading datasets to your local workstation. ---

Now that you understand the core flow of Brainlife Connects: Explore ezBIDS to standardize raw scanner data into BIDS. Read the Pipeline Guide to automate large cohort workflows. Learn how to wrap your own analysis scripts in the App Developer Guide. Have questions or need assistance? Join the Brainlife Slack Community or ask SKAI directly in Brainlife Connects!

ezBIDS is a web-based BIDS conversion tool that requires neither installation, programming proficiency, nor knowledge of the Unix terminal and BIDS specification. The term BIDS is an acronym that stands for the Brain Imaging Data Structure. More specifically, BIDS is a format for describing and organizing (primarily neuroimaging) data, greatly enhancing data sharing within the scientific community, as well as enabling access to a suite of processing and analysis tools that can be automatically executed on BIDS data, known as BIDS apps. This documentation provides an in-depth description of ezBIDS's functionality for converting data to BIDS. If you are new to ezBIDS and would like to see a simple use case of ezBIDS, please refer to the ezBIDS tutorial.

The process of converting raw imaging data to BIDS is often time-consuming and can require substantial technical expertise. Furthermore, the BIDS specification, the rules governing how data must be described and organized, are complex and can be daunting for researchers relatively unfamiliar with BIDS. While there exist numerous tools for assisting users convert their data to BIDS (for complete lists, see here and here), these tools largely require a level of techninal experise and knowledge of BIDS. ezBIDS was designed to alleviate these requirements. Specifically, ezBIDS provides unique features that differentiate it from other BIDS conversion tools: 1. No installation or programming required. It works in your web browser. 2. Semi-automated inference and guidance for BIDS adherence. It makes educated guesses about how your data should be mapped into BIDS and proposes both initial BIDS mapping of your data and warnings on the things that might need your attention. 3. Conversion of task event/timing files associated with functional BOLD (func/bold) sequences. If you have collected data using a task ezBIDS will help you map your tasks events into BIDS. 4. Multiple data management options: Download BIDS-converted data to a local computer or server. Push BIDS-converted data to open-science archives and platforms, such as OpenNeuro.org and brainlife.io. Think about ezBIDS as a small, smart, decision support system. ezBIDS attempts to do the heavy lifting for users, interpreting t

Start by uploading your raw neuroimaging data to ezBIDS. Supported formats include DICOM and NIfTI. The platform will read your data and help you organize it according to the BIDS specification. Upon reaching the ezBIDS homepage, users can click on the "Get Started" button to begin converting their data. Users are then routed to the ezBIDS upload page, where imaging data will be uploaded to a secure server. Additional information regarding this upload process as it pertains to data access and control can be found here. Once uploaded, users are guided through several steps (i.e., web pages) to ensure that data are accurately described, organized, pseudonymized, and, ultimately, converted. These steps are described below: For ezBIDS to access users' imaging data, the data must first be uploaded to ezBIDS's secure and encrypted server (ezBIDS runs on a secure VM running on the HIPAA-aligned National Science Foundation's Jetstream-Cloud). There are two accepted upload methods: Raw DICOM data from the scanner or imaging device. NIfTI/JSON data converted from DICOMs using dcm2niix. If using this option, it is best if the most recent dcm2niix version was used. Data privacy Uploaded data can only be accessed through the unique URL with your session ID. Also, uploaded data are purged from the ezBIDS system after 5 days. ezBIDS prefers that non-anonymized data are uploaded (e.g. with the -ba y flag option in dcm2niix), as this makes it easier to discern the subject (and session, if app

This page allows users to provide general information regarding their dataset, such as authors, funding sources, etc. Users only need to provide information here the first time using ezBIDS with data from a new dataset. When using ezBIDS with newly acquired data from the same dataset as before, this information is already provided and is therefore redundant to specify again. Progress checks For this and subsequent ezBIDS web pages, certain information is required by BIDS, indicated on each page with a red asterisk or circle. These fields must be entered, otherwise, users will be unable to progress to the next page. This provides users with real-time assistance on what information is required in order to have BIDS-compliant data, rather than going through the entire process only to learn afterward that there is an issue to resolve.

On this page, ezBIDS provides the subject (and session, if applicable) IDs of the uploaded data. Users may edit or modify these fields as they see fit. This can either be done manually or by selecting an option within the "Reset Subject Mapping" button.

ezBIDS organizes all uploaded data into specific series and group IDs (grouping data). This is an intermediate step, that ezBIDS uses to facilitate editing entire series (or groups) of data files. Say, you want to change all the files from a single subject so that all the files start with a specific subject ID, or say you want to change all the data that are anatomical to start with the prefix anat, ezBIDS allows you to do that by grouping data for you by subjects, series, etc. Grouping procedure ezBIDS makes educated guesses about your data using information saved in the DICOM files. ezBIDS uses the DICOM fields Series Description, Image Type, Echo Time, and Repetition Time to group data together. This means that ezBIDS assumes that data with the matching values in these fields are part of the same series of data. ezBIDS then matches the Series to the corresponding BIDS entities. This grouping procedure saves users' time by serving files that might need to undergo similar changes in groups. ezBIDS provides warning messages (yellow circle and asterisk) to explain how the data were grouped. If this is incorrect and needs fixing, users can modify the groups using the graphical interface. If ezBIDS fails to group some of the data files, it will default to exclude the files, indicating that the files will not be converted to BIDS. Users may adjust this if necessary (or even mark data files not excluded by exBIDS as 'to be excluded', e.g., localizer sequences). If a BIDS entity la

A critical feature of ezBIDS is the ability to support tasks and event files. If users collected functional BOLD (func/bold) data and have the corresponding timing files. The following are timing files formats compatible with ezBIDS: .csv, .tsv, .txt, .out, and .xlsx. A graphical interface guides the user in matching the files to BIDS structures. Importantly, ezBIDS comes with a beta feature and built-in compatibility with E-Prime files. When uploading timing files, it is crucial that the following entity labels be explicitly specified: subject, (session, if applicable), task, and run. These must match the corresponding func/bold sequences. This information can either be provided in the file path or as columns in the timing data themselves. Failure to do so will result in ezBIDS creating a placeholder value for any mismatched entity labels that will later require manual intervention. ezBIDS assists users in dealing with timing events and units BIDS requires that timing files be translated into events.tsv format, with several required and optional columns. Required columns include the onset and duration. ezBIDS has the ability to assist users in cases where uploaded timing files do not have a column that specifically pertains to onset and duration. For example, rather than a column specifying trial durations, a file might contain a column for trialonset and another column for trialoffset. Users can specify an arithmetic method (Subtract, Add) and choose the two columns that wh

Upon reaching this page, all individual imaging sequences are provided in the order they were collected for each subject’s (and session’s) scan. Here, users can make edits/modifications to individual files (e.g., set a sequence to exclude due to known participant motion, etc.) that were otherwise not possible when Grouping data. All modifications made on the Series Mapping and Events pages are applied. ezBIDS applies a run entity label to sequences if there were multiple occurrences during the scan. Functional data exclusion ezBIDS applies a volume threshold on 4D data (e.g., func/bold) to check for sequences that might have had to be restarted during the scan. The threshold is calculated based on the expected number of volumes collected during a 60-sec period, given the TR (60/TR). If a 4D sequence does not meet this threshold, ezBIDS sets the datatype/suffix pair to exclude, unless modified by the user.

Users have the option (recommended) to deface all anatomical images in order to further anonymize the data. ezBIDS provides two defacing procedures: Quickshear and pyDeface. Depending on the number of anatomical files in the uploaded data, this process may take several minutes, though ezBIDS can parallelize this process with concurrent defacing processes. If the defacing is suboptimal (i.e. defacing cuts into the brain itself), users may try again with the other defacing option or simply specify that they do not wish to deface the anatomical data.

For each subject ID specified, users may specify phenotypical information pertaining to each participant. By default, ezBIDS attempts to provide the sex and age of participants if this information is present in the metadata (typically only specified if non-anonymized data are uploaded). Users may add additional columns (e.g., handedness) or delete existing columns.

At this stage, users can click on the green "Finalize" button for ezBIDS to apply all user edits/modifications to create a BIDS-compliant dataset. Users may elect to keep any data that was set to “exclude” if they so choose. Once complete, two screens are presented. On the left is a Linux tree structure showing the BIDS dataset organization and file names. On the right is a screen output of the bids-validator, which provides a final check to ensure that the data are BIDS compliant. Any validator warnings appear in yellow and can be ignored (but it's good practice to resolve these at some point), and errors appear in red, indicating that the dataset is not BIDS-compliant for some specified reason and requires correction. If users need or wish to return to previous pages for additional edits/modifications they may do so. Then, upon returning to this page, users must click the green "Rerun Finalize Step" to apply all new changes. Once a BIDS-compliant dataset is generated, users can click on the blue "Download BIDS" button to download their zipped data to their local computer/server, and/or send their BIDS data to OpenNeuro.org or brainlife.io. Downloading non-BIDS compliant data Users may still download their BIDS dataset (or upload it elsewhere) even if the bids-validator returns error(s); however, users should know that their dataset is not fully BIDS-compliant and will need to be corrected at some point. Lastly, upon completing the BIDS mapping, ezBIDS automatically generate

ezBIDS provides additional features to assist users in converting their data to BIDS. 1. ezBIDS configuration templates ezBIDS creates templates for scanning sessions. Any scanning session processed using ezBIDS can become a template for future sessions. ezBIDS Templates can be reused to automatically load the BIDS mapping configuration a user has identified. Templates are helpful in the common situation where the same scanning protocol is used for multiple sessions. Often, researchers set up a scanning protocol and configure a series of scans to be acquired on multiple subjects across the duration of a research project. When the scans from the first subject are uploaded and processed via ezBIDS the researcher is effectively creating an ezBIDS Template, automatically. ezBIDS Templates are JSON files created every time a dataset is processed via ezBIDS. To use the template all the user has to do is download the template and upload the template with any new sessions acquired in the future. ezBIDS Templates can be reused for any number of datasets and reduce users' interaction with the ezBIDS graphical interface. More specifically, after ezBIDS has converted a dataset to BIDS, users have the option to download the file ezBIDStemplate.json. This file contains all information, to map the DICOMs to BIDS, including user edits and modifications, from the ezBIDS session. This file can be uploaded with new datasets. When done so, the information in the file is applied to the new ezBIDS

ezBIDS provides BIDS conversion support for the following data modalities: 1. MRI       - Including arterial spin labeling (ASL)       - Including functional bold task events 2. DWI 3. PET       - Including blood recording data 4. MEG PET and MEG Support for these modalities are relatively new and in the beta stage. Improvements will continue as users submit issues pertaining to to bugs and other related requests. ---

Although ezBIDS is a web-based service that does not require installation, it is possible to install it on your local machine or server. The main advantage here is that data is not uploaded to the ezBIDS server (i.e. data remains on-site). Instead, data is copied to one of the ezBIDS containers (brainlife_ezbids-handler) at /tmp/ezbids-workdir. However, with this approach users cannot upload their finalized BIDS-compliant data to brainlife.io via ezBIDS, as this requires authentication that isn't available with a local installation. Furthermore, setting up ezBIDS locally may require some technical know-how. The following steps should enable you to successfully install ezBIDS. Step 1: Software prerequisites Make sure the following software packages are installed on your computer: 1. Docker 2. Docker Compose 3. Node(.js) & npm Node and npm installation Download the LTS version (20.11.0), as ezBIDS does not work well with newer Node versions. If working on Mac OS, avoid downloading from homebrew, as homebrew provides the most recent version or puts an older version in an atypical directory (e.g. node@20). To check that they are in your $PATH, enter "software --version" (e.g. docker --version) into your terminal. If successfully installed, a version ID will be displayed. ezBIDS is a community-drive project, and as such, contributions are both welcome and encouraged. For technical contributions, it is highly recommended that users locally install ezBIDS on their machine (see Installing ezBIDS locally section for details) and submit a PR for bug fixes and feature enhancements.
